items.title: A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age.

items.title: DIY Meshtastic Solar Node: Muziworks Uno Full Build Guide
items.content_html:
A bare Meshtastic board, a battery and a solar panel are a good start. To turn them into something I can leave outside, I want a proper enclosure, a secure mounting arrangement, an external antenna and sealed cable entries. 

For this build, I’m using the Elecrow Muziworks Muzi Base Uno. I already had the small solar panel wired up and the basic configuration working. Now I’m putting everything into a weatherproof case, updating the firmware and getting the node ready for an outdoor test. 

The big question is the solar panel. It is very small, and I’m not yet convinced it will keep the battery charged. This is a working build ready for testing, not a proven, indefinitely self-sufficient solar installation. 

 


Key Takeaways


	Update and verify the firmware before enclosing the board, while USB access is easy.
	Plan the internal layout around USB clearance, battery-connector access and safe assembly.
	Seal every new enclosure opening, including the solar-wire entry behind the panel.
	Successful mesh communication does not prove the small solar panel can sustain the node.



Table of Contents


	Parts and Layout
	Update the Meshtastic Firmware First
	Make a Small 3D-Printed Board Mount
	Prepare the Enclosure and External Connections
	Mount the Board and Battery
	Route, Solder and Attach the Solar Panel
	Seal the Cable Entry and Check the Finished Layout
	Configure the Node for a Fixed Installation
	Run a Traceroute Before Mounting Outside
	Put It Outside and Test the Solar Side


Parts and Layout

The Uno does not have the Wi-Fi capability of the Duo, which suits what I want from this solar node. It also came with a small three-wire battery, including a sensing wire rather than just the usual positive and negative connections. 

Here is what I used: 


	Muzi Base Uno and its supplied battery.
	A weatherproof enclosure with rear mounting hardware and an internal mounting plate.
	A small solar panel, already connected during the earlier setup.
	An SMA male to N female bulkhead adapter for the external antenna connection.
	A larger 915 MHz external antenna.
	A gasketed enclosure breather plug.
	A custom 3D-printed board mount, small screws, 3M double-sided mounting tape and silicone sealant.


The linked parts are affiliate links, which means I may earn from qualifying purchases. 

Before fixing anything down, check the whole layout. The board needs room for its antenna connection, battery plug and solar wiring. Just as importantly, leave enough clearance to connect a USB cable for future firmware updates. A neat installation is not much use if you have to dismantle it every time you need access. 

Update the Meshtastic Firmware First

I did the firmware update before putting the board in the enclosure. It is much easier to work with the USB connection while everything is still on the bench. 

Connect the antenna before powering the board. I kept that same order later when connecting the battery. 


	Connect the Uno to the computer with a USB cable.
	Open the Meshtastic web flasher at flasher.meshtastic.org.
	Select Muziworks, then the Muzi Base Uno/Duo device entry.
	Select the firmware version and start the flashing process.
	Follow the prompt to put the nRF-based board into DFU mode.
	When the board appears as a removable drive, download the matching UF2 firmware file.
	Copy the UF2 file onto that drive and wait for the transfer to finish.


I chose Meshtastic 2.8.2 alpha for this build. That was a deliberate choice to try the newer firmware, not a recommendation to treat an alpha release as stable. The flasher offered different release channels, so check what you are selecting rather than simply assuming the newest option is the best one. 

Before copying the new firmware over, I also saved a copy of the existing UF2 file from the device drive to my computer. That gave me a local copy of the old firmware. I would not treat that as a separate backup of all the device settings. 

Once the copy completed, the drive ejected and disappeared as the board restarted. I reconnected in the Meshtastic app and checked the device details. The firmware version now showed 2.8.2, which confirmed the update had worked. 


Take an Initial Noise Reading


The newer firmware exposed an antenna noise reading that I wanted to try. With the little stock antenna attached, the app reported approximately -97 dBm and displayed the result in green. 

That gave me a useful starting point before changing the enclosure and antenna. It is a noise-floor reading, though, not a range test or a measurement of antenna gain. For noise, a more negative value means a lower noise level: -97 dBm is quieter than -83 dBm. 

Make a Small 3D-Printed Board Mount

I like mounting the board on a small raised plate rather than fixing it directly against the bottom of the enclosure. It keeps the installation tidier and leaves some space underneath the components. 

For this one, I drew a basic sketch with the dimensions I needed and used AI to help turn it into a printable mount. The result was an STL file that I opened in the slicer, checked and printed in PETG. 

 

The mounting-hole spacing came out correctly, and the board fitted the printed part. I used three small screws to secure it. 

The printed mount is optional. What matters is keeping the board secure, clear of the enclosure floor and accessible enough to maintain. There was one detail I would improve in another version: make the battery connector easier to reach after the board is mounted. That became awkward during assembly. 

Prepare the Enclosure and External Connections

I have used this style of enclosure on other outdoor nodes without problems, so it is a familiar starting point. The supplied brackets attach to the back for mounting against a wall or another support. 

The case also came with cable-entry fittings, but I did not need those for this layout. Instead, I made openings for: 


	The antenna bulkhead at the top.
	The breather plug on the side.
	The solar-panel wires behind the panel.


I drilled the antenna and breather openings first. The solar-wire hole came later in my assembly, although planning all the openings before installing the electronics would make the job simpler. 


Fit the Breather Plug


The breather plug is there to help manage moisture inside the enclosure. I am not using it as a cooling vent. 

It passes through the side wall and tightens against a rubber gasket. I seated the gasket against the case and tightened the fitting so it sat securely. 


Fit the Antenna Bulkhead


The antenna connection uses an SMA male to N female bulkhead arrangement. Check the actual connector contacts as well as the threads: in this build, the SMA pin mates with the socket on the board’s antenna connection. 

The bulkhead passes through the top of the enclosure and has its own rubber gasket. Tightening the retaining hardware compresses that gasket against the case. 


The antenna and breather fittings are in place before the electronics go into the case.


I then fitted the larger 915 MHz antenna to the outside. The N connector gives me a substantial external connection rather than leaving the small board-level connection exposed. 

Mount the Board and Battery

With the external fittings installed, I checked the internal layout again. I positioned the printed mount low enough in the case to preserve USB access, with the battery beside it and room to route the antenna and solar wiring. 

I used two strips of 3M double-sided tape beneath the printed mount. I have had good results with this tape on other outdoor builds, so I used it again for the mount, battery and panel. 

Getting the backing off the tape is usually the part that tests my patience. This time, it was not too bad. 

The more important difficulty was the battery connector. I initially had the board attached to the mount, then removed it again because I was bending the cable and making the assembly awkward to handle. With the mount fixed down, I connected the antenna, plugged in the battery and taped the battery into the middle of the case. 

Everything fitted, but reinstalling the board screws while it was powered made me uncomfortable. A dropped screw could short the board. 

That is the part of this assembly I would change: finish the screw work with power disconnected. A better connector-access cutout in the mount, or a suitable power switch, would make the build much easier to work on. There is no prize for trying to balance tiny screws over a live board. 

Route, Solder and Attach the Solar Panel

The panel sits on the outside of the lid. To get its wires through the enclosure, I disconnected the panel leads, drilled a small hole behind its intended position and passed the wires through. 

I then soldered the leads back onto the panel, keeping positive and negative on their correct connections. 


	Check the panel position against the lid.
	Route the wires through the opening behind the panel.
	Reconnect the positive and negative leads.
	Check that the wires and solder joints do not prevent the panel from sitting properly.
	Attach the panel with mounting tape.
	Seal the wire opening with silicone.


I ran into a small problem here: the solder connection on the back of the panel stood proud enough to stop it sitting flat against the lid. The first two strips of tape did not provide enough clearance. 

I adjusted the mounting with additional tape so the panel could sit properly without rocking on the solder joint. It is worth checking that clearance before pressing the adhesive down firmly. 

The panel’s rating was not clearly established during this build, so I am not going to give it a definite wattage or current specification. It is simply a very small panel, and its ability to keep this node running still needs an outdoor test. 

Seal the Cable Entry and Check the Finished Layout

The antenna bulkhead and breather plug have gaskets, but the solar-wire hole needs separate sealing. I used silicone around that opening to keep water from entering along the wires. 

The hole is behind the solar panel, which gives it some shelter, but that is not a substitute for sealing it. 

 

Before closing the lid, I checked the main items: 


	The board and battery were secured.
	The antenna connection was attached.
	The solar leads were connected and routed inside the case.
	The USB port remained accessible.
	The external fittings were tightened and the wire entry was sealed.


At this point, the node was assembled in an enclosure intended for outdoor use. That is different from having a verified waterproof rating for the modified build. The drilled openings and seals still need to hold up in practice. 

Configure the Node for a Fixed Installation

Back in the Meshtastic app, I requested another noise reading with the external antenna connected. It returned approximately -97 dBm, much like the stock antenna reading on the bench. 

That was encouraging, but it did not demonstrate a range improvement. The node was still indoors, and a noise reading alone cannot tell me how well a rooftop installation will perform. 

I initially left the device in Client mode. For this fixed-node experiment, I then changed the role to Client Base, selected the option to rebroadcast everything and saved the settings. 

The node restarted and reappeared in the app. Those are the settings I chose for this installation, rather than a claim that every solar-powered Meshtastic node should use exactly the same configuration. 

Run a Traceroute Before Mounting Outside

For a basic connectivity check, I tried a traceroute to a nearby node down the street. The request reached it directly, while the reply came back through a different path. 

That confirmed the assembled node could communicate on the mesh. I then stood the enclosure upright so the antenna was vertical instead of lying along the desk and repeated the test. 

The displayed link reading improved from roughly -11 dB to -9 dB. It was a useful reminder to test the antenna in its intended orientation, but it was still only a short bench check, not a measured outdoor range test. 

Put It Outside and Test the Solar Side

For the first outdoor trial, I mounted the enclosure on the side of my garden shed. This is not its final position. I wanted an accessible place to see whether the whole assembly worked before moving it to a roof. 


The shed mount is a temporary test position before a possible roof installation.


By then, the solar-panel mounting had been sorted out, the case was closed and the node was running. Firmware flashing, the external antenna connection and the initial mesh checks had all worked. 

The unresolved part is the energy budget. I need to leave it outside over the next few days and find out whether that little panel can keep up with the node’s consumption. 

For now, I have a tidy, enclosed Meshtastic solar-node build ready for that test. If the panel proves too small, that will be the next thing to change. Getting the hardware assembled is one milestone; proving that it can stay running outside is the next one.

items.title: Google disrupts Android botnet affecting over 1.3 million devices, bans manufacturer
items.content_html:
Google and its partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, which used a backdoor on more than 1.3 million Android devices, and banned Chinese manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co. from making certified Android products. Google alleges Videostrong deliberately embedded the malware in device firmware and sold criminal affiliates access for ad fraud, proxy services and installation of other malware. Infected devices included TV boxes, digital signage, karaoke machines and telehealth equipment.

The operation shut down command servers used by XCPE and related malware families, which Google said could cut off access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices. The takedown did not remove XCPE from device firmware: the malware can reinstall after a reboot, and the backdoor remains unless manufacturers or platforms take action or owners replace the devices. Google says it has strengthened its firmware review process after finding that the malware was loaded after devices first booted.
